wulf_published.facility: Muskie Data campus electric service, Grayson, KY (incl. Big Sandy 760 MW CCGT)

source_notes.note: Customer is 'a subsidiary of Meta Platforms, Inc.'. The ESA was disclosed with the October 2024 application (no exact day, so 'announced' is YYYY-MM). The LPSC accepted the settlement in August 2025; Entergy's 2025-08-20 approval release gives no MW.
'More than' 5,200 MW. Utility-built generation that still needs LPSC certification (still under review in July 2026 reports); counted as pending, not signed, until approved.

'Up to' 3 GW. The IURC approved it in June 2026, and the technology (combined-cycle gas) comes from NiSource's Q2-2026 10-Q, both in the same evidence file. The 3 GW figure covers more than the CCGT; secondary sources say two 1,300 MW CCGTs plus 400 MW BESS, which is unverified. A 7/17/26 filing amends the service agreement and GenCo PPA to raise Amazon's contracted load by 400 MW, with a final IURC order sought by November 2026 (NiSource Q2'26 call, docs/research/evidence/2026-10-17-cap-amzn-nwindiana-nipsco.txt); not a separate row.
The only source is VoltaGrid's release. Oracle's own newsroom post was not found.

Doubles the earlier 500 MW contracted demand (that agreement's date is not verified here). The amended contract still needs Kentucky PSC approval, so the 1 GW row is pending. TeraWulf pays the estimated financing costs of Kentucky Power's planned 760 MW combined-cycle plant at Big Sandy, hence gas.

Definitive agreements effective 9/30/26 with terms through 2048. Black Hills plans 564 MW (nameplate) of new natural gas generation at its Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station; the other 26 MW comes from market purchases and tariff service (same release, in the evidence file). The project's 2.7 GW resource mix also includes ~2.1 GW of third-party contracted resources managed under the LPCS tariff; those are not a row (AEP's 702 MW fuel cells are a separate row and may be among them).

output.title: Synthetic hub power is up 50% on the year while Henry Hub gas is flat
output.detail: Over the same 30 days a megawatt-hour there cost as much as 30.0 MMBtu of gas, against 20.0 a year earlier — 4.0× a combined-cycle plant's fuel bill. The fuel did not move the price; the grid did.
